testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Effect of releasing Indians from Government control
testimony.key_claims: Sound judgment has not always been exercised in granting fee patents; many recipients have not used the privilege wisely. Young, old and uneducated Indians should be protected as long as possible. Approximately three-fifths of the total area of five reservations (452,807-453,807 acres) is now restricted. This reduction occurred within past twenty years and another twenty years will see restricted holdings nearly eliminated. Indian hospitality culture where visitors must be fed discourages individual advancement. After Oneida land was patented and sold, each family placed on own resources and sponging largely ceased. Indian education expenditures of five millions annually should qualify substantial number for citizenship. Chief concern should be with the young (ages 18-45) and with old and untrained. Not moving too fast in the matter overall, doing fair and prudent thing.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Record of patent-in-fee Indians on Ponca Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Record of patent-in-fee Indians on Ponca Reservation is not good. As a rule they either sell the patented land or mortgage it immediately, sometimes before the patent is issued. They spend proceeds on high-powered automobiles and non-essentials as well as booze and extracts, then go back to parents, working a hardship on older Indians. Restricted Indians are making a living from their lands by leasing for agricultural, oil and gas purposes. No Indian over 45 should be given patent-in-fee. Young able-bodied competent male Indians educated at Government expense should be given patents. Three-fourths of young adult Indians have received patents and it has done them harm instead of good. Old Indians and minors still in trust are fairly prosperous and happy.

testimony.witness_title: Clerk in Charge, Kaw Sub-agency, 34 years in Service
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Indians who have had restrictions removed - Kaw tribe
testimony.key_claims: Kaw Treaty specifies Indians shall make applications for certificates in writing, which many don't want to do. It is usually the incompetent who makes the most effort to get restrictions removed. Great care should be exercised in removing restrictions on Indian lands. Provided detailed list showing the vast majority of Kaw Indians who received certificates of competency sold their land and spent the money. About 25 Kaws are perfectly competent but have not asked for certificates. Speculators and land grafters profit from the foolishness of those who get certificates. Homestead allotments of old Indians, those not in good health, girls, and women with children or no-account husbands should be held under Government restrictions. Many times when Indian woman loses property she loses husband.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Fee patent Indians at Tonkawa
testimony.key_claims: In eleven years of service, knows of only one patent-in-fee Indian accumulating any property (Lona Ciserneos, credit given to hard-working Mexican husband). Robert Tah, Railroad Cisco and David Williams received fee patents within last three years and immediately converted lands to money, purchased expensive automobiles, Indian toggery, gambling and high living. Now in bad way living from money they can wheedle from relatives. Condition of fee patent Indians not as good as when under Government jurisdiction. Tribe has less and many have to live on what little is left. Old dependent Indians receiving $100 monthly scarcely able to exist. Indians generally not satisfied with what has been done for them. Many think Government employees are in league with grafters. Would recommend turning able-bodied Indians loose reserving 20 acres for home, establishing old and uneducated under community system.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Otoe Sub-agency, Red Rock, Oklahoma
testimony.subject: Condition of Indians before and after receiving patents-in-fee
testimony.key_claims: Fee patent Indians are in worse condition than when under Government jurisdiction. Indians who received patents sold land, bought expensive automobiles, spent money on gambling. Old dependent Indians receiving $100 monthly can scarcely exist. Indians are dissatisfied and believe government employees are in league with grafters. Recommends turning loose able-bodied and educated Indians but establishing community system for uneducated and old dependent ones with 20 acres reserved for home. Successful examples include Harold Barnes, Jacob Blackhawk, James Arkeketa, Henry Black, George W. Dailey, Blaine Faw Faw, David Pettit, Berth Tillman, Sam Lincoln.

testimony.subject: Fee patent Indians at Pawnee
testimony.key_claims: Indians questioned about release from federal control stated they are not satisfied, in bad financial shape, and feel government should not have released them. Indians mortgaged or sold land immediately upon receiving patent-in-fee, purchased expensive autos and lived high. Suggests older Indians be kept under government control while younger Indians should be given competency rights. Believes sooner younger Indians are released, sooner Indian problem will be solved. Suggests reserving 40 acres of original allotment as home site.

testimony.witness_title: Agent Farmer, Pawnee Agency, Pawnee, Oklahoma
testimony.subject: Fee patent Indians at Pawnee
testimony.key_claims: Indians who received fee patents sold land and spent all money, are in debt. Very few who received patents still own their allotments - not one out of ten have not sold. Recommends issuing fee patent for part of allotment and holding at least 40 acres in trust. Names of those doing well: Louis Matlock, Elmo Jim, Eva N. Cummings. Names of those who have not gained: Clarance Field, Wallace Murie, Caroline Murie, Maggie Knife Chief, Thomas Hand, John Howell, Maude Hand. Those doing well who still hold land: Emmit Pearson, George Gover, Frank Rouwalk.

testimony.subject: Patented Indians - Sac & Fox and Iowa Indians
testimony.key_claims: Patented Indians have disposed of allotments and are compelled to labor. Not as easy for Indian to secure position as white man. One Indian worked for one company for three or four years. About 81 patents given out four or five years ago, not more than 10 still have their land. Some heired lands remain. Children do not have necessaries of life. Does not think advisable to turn all Indians loose at once. Suggests allowing Indians to dispose of heired lands but hold own allotments.

testimony.subject: Cheyenne and Arapahoe Indians and fee patents
testimony.key_claims: Has worked three years with Cheyenne and Arapahoe Indians. Knows of only a few who kept land after receiving patent. Nearly all sell as soon as they can make sale, spend money, are satisfied, go to work and make better citizens. Does not think it good policy to turn all Indians loose from Government control at once. Suggests young boys and girls who finish education should have property turned over. Indians should be expected to take care of themselves. Lists Indians farming successfully under government control: David Bighead, Harry Bates, Walter Fire, Dan Tucker.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Spokane Indian Agency, Wellpinit, Washington
testimony.subject: Fee patents and releasing Indians from Government supervision on Spokane Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Pretty well in accord with Office policy but does not think good to make all Indians of half or less Indian blood citizens at once. Each case should be decided on merits considering educational qualifications, business experience, degree of Indian blood, robustness, and age. Spokane allotments mostly 80 acres, not good quality, mostly timber. Many allotments worth only $400-$800. Recommends 20-40 acres held in trust for home site. 112 Indians received fee patents; 54 retained allotments, 48 sold them. Most sold soon after receiving patents. Indians who retained land are generally doing as well as before.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Spokane Indian Agency, Wellpinit, Washington
testimony.subject: Condition of patent-in-fee Indians on Spokane Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Larger percent of fee patent Indians doing as well as before. Quite a few sold land but larger percent used money to good advantage. Percentage who spent money without good returns no larger than any other race. Most are satisfied with patents. Would use same policy Department has been using, examine each individual case. Would release all allotments on this reservation because each is small. Provides names and addresses of those who sold and those who retained land.

testimony.witness_title: Field Clerk, United States Indian Service, Poteau, Oklahoma
testimony.subject: Full removal of restrictions on Choctaw Indians in Five Tribes
testimony.key_claims: Government work in Five Tribes has been to divide common estate and vest individually. Future business will be with individuals. Should focus on fitting individual Indian for life in competition. Quantum of Indian blood alone should not determine management. Some full-bloods have better business sense than those of small degree of Indian blood. Character, education, business experience, environment, age, and all circumstances should be considered. Considerable number should have restrictions retained indefinitely. Estimates between 50 and 75 percent have made a success. Most failures come from 'easy money' attitude. Successes due to simple homely virtues.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Kiowa Indian Agency, Anadarko, Oklahoma
testimony.subject: Patents-in-fee at Kiowa Indian Agency
testimony.key_claims: Most important administrative function is deciding whether to recommend patent-in-fee. Granting control of estate prematurely subjects Indian to temptation and extravagant habits. Believes it is grossest mistake to issue patents based on blood status or educational qualifications alone. Has many full-blood Indians who cannot speak English whom he would rather trust with patent than educated young fellows. Of last sixty patents from Declaration of Policy, twenty were promptly mortgaged (only one released), sixteen sold outright, twenty-four clear but likely to be encumbered. In more than six years, can recall only one case of success. Recommends original allotment or at least 40 acres be inalienable during life of allottee with land taxable after trust period. Better to err by delaying patent than granting prematurely.

testimony.subject: Issuance of patents to Indians
testimony.key_claims: Convinced that reports of Indians selling lands and wasting proceeds are only too true, and probably only a portion of the full story. Going too fast in releasing Indians from government supervision and protection.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, United States Indian Service, Shawnee, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on fee patents
testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee policy and Indian land management
testimony.key_claims: Of last 60 patents issued under Declaration of Policy, 20 were promptly mortgaged (only 1 released), 16 tracts sold outright, 24 still clear but expected to be encumbered. Cannot recall but one case in six years where an Indian successfully handled his land with a patent. Recommended 40-acre inalienable homestead from each 160-acre allotment. Advocated reimbursable agreements over patents. Described loan agent soliciting land transactions before patents were issued, using William Panther (Billy Hood, Shawnee No. 351) and John Pecan as examples. Opposed using blood status or educational qualifications alone as basis for competency. Stated Indians do not care to crawl before they walk and want expensive implements. Noted that the patent is never asked for until the applicant has a plan to alienate the land.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on fee patents
testimony.subject: Granting of fee patents to Indians
testimony.key_claims: Over 500 Indians on his reservation released from Government control; very few made good. Many sold lands and homes and squandered money. Opposed rapid release from Federal control. Opposed granting citizenship to Indians in bulk. Believed competent Indians should classify reservation Indians in harmony with superintendent with rigid examination. Supported holding 40 acres in trust as nontaxable homestead. Opposed professional agitator societies calling for abolition of Indian Bureau. Noted American Legion's position that ex-Indian soldiers should be citizens, but many ex-service boys now without lands. Stated Department going too fast in releasing Indians.

testimony.witness_title: Acting Field Clerk, Tahlequah, Oklahoma, Cherokee Indians, Five Civilized Tribes
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Advisability of granting patents-in-fee and releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.key_claims: Impossible to apply hard and fast rule to all Indians alike. Indiscriminate policy of releasing every Indian of half or less blood without supervision would be criminally unjust and disastrous. Competent full-blood Indians exist who can handle affairs; many mixed-bloods need strict supervision. Competent Indians rarely apply for restriction removal because restricted lands are not taxable and they value their homes. Ten percent whose restrictions were removed by competency board sold lands and misused proceeds; ninety percent made good. Of those making good: 30% decided success, 50% indifferent success, 10% barely escape failure, 10% complete failure. Training and education are key factors in success. Full-blood Indian does not seem to realize value of money.

testimony.witness_title: Supervisor of restricted Indians, Five Civilized Tribes
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from government supervision
testimony.subject: Competency and success rates of Indians released from government control
testimony.key_claims: Spent lifetime among restricted class Indians; 30% of released Indians making decided success; 50% succeeding indifferently; 10% barely escaping failure; 10% failed completely. Education is the primary factor determining success or failure. Competent Indians rarely apply for restriction removal because restricted lands are not taxable and they value their homes. Recommended competency commission release competent Indians regardless of their wishes. 10% of those released by competency board sold lands and misused proceeds while 90% made good.

testimony.witness_title: Field Clerk, Five Civilized Tribes, Okmulgee, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from government supervision
testimony.subject: Views on releasing Indians from government supervision
testimony.key_claims: 46 years old, enrolled Chickasaw member, lifelong resident among Five Civilized Tribes. Prior to allotment Indians had little knowledge of land value and held land in common. Notes and mortgages were unknown among Indians. Act of May 27, 1908 left Indians facing new conditions without experience - long on land but short on money. Indians were easily led to part with land. Full-blood Indians do not realize value of money. At least 90% of allottees lease surplus land for only a fraction of rental value. Money is soon spent and squandered. Inherited lands sold at prices far below real value with only county court approval. Probate court proceedings are only ministerial not judicial. 75% or more of inherited lands sold for 50% or less of real value. Recommended legislation requiring Department approval for conveyance of deceased allottees' lands. Recommended compelling Indian children to attend public schools. Recommended guardians furnish certificate of ward's school attendance.

testimony.witness_title: Field Clerk, Five Civilized Tribes, Holdenville, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from government supervision
testimony.subject: Removal of restrictions and winding up Indian affairs
testimony.key_claims: Turning loose Indians by degree of blood or school grade is inadvisable because many enrolled as less than full-blood are actually full-blood. Knows one instance where an Indian enrolled as one-eighth blood is actually full-blood and speaks no English. At least 75% of those with restrictions removed have disposed of allotments. Really competent Indians do not desire restrictions removed; it is the incompetent who do. Successful Indians in district were arbitrarily removed by competency commission two or three years ago. Recommended each case decided on merits. Recommended Congress enact law retaining sufficient acreage for homestead and allowing sale of remainder with proceeds used for improvements and farming equipment.

testimony.witness_title: Field Clerk, Five Civilized Tribes, Ardmore, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from government supervision
testimony.subject: Policy of granting patents-in-fee to Chickasaw Indians
testimony.key_claims: Policy of granting patents-in-fee has been premature in many cases. Trust created by Congress has not been kept as intended; injury instead of good has resulted. Removal of restrictions should be decided on merits, not quantum of blood. Many less-than-half-blood Indians are less fit than many full-bloods. Too much liberality in general removal evident; many became prey of designing men. Only a small percentage have made success in full meaning. Recommended reserving at least one-fourth of homestead allotments of average value, held inalienable during allottee's lifetime. Recommended more careful disposition of applications for removal.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from government supervision
testimony.subject: Releasing Indians from government supervision at Crow Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Prepared tabular statement on patent-in-fee Indians. Endorsed views of field employees and missionaries, especially W.A. Petzoldt's letter which closely matched his own opinion. Indian must be put on his own responsibility; nursing process will not prepare him. Does not believe in wholesale policy that would cause suffering among old people. Young men and women with schooling should be given their portion and told it is 'root hog or die.'

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.subject: Condition of patent-in-fee Indians on Crow Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Out of 301 Indians, reports made on 140: 54 held their land (10 with mortgages), 84 (60%) sold all land, 2 sold part. Of 105 Indians assessed: some classed good/fair, some same, some worse/poor. 77 Indians' land money disposition tracked. Recommended forcing responsibility on younger educated Indians while protecting old. Proposed capitalizing tribal property and buying out individuals' interest.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.subject: Assessment of fee patent Indians' condition
testimony.key_claims: Majority of fee patent Indians financially worse off. Most have very little inclination for work and little business experience. If all Indians given full control, 95% would be paupers in less than three years. Fee patent Indians cannot compete with average white man. Doubted whether giving any Indian fee patent without first learning their ability was wise.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.subject: Policy recommendations for fee patents
testimony.key_claims: Percentage of Indians who made good considerably smaller than failures. Full-bloods more capable and dependable than mixed-bloods. Recommended individual case examination, holding at least 40 acres inalienable as homestead. Older uneducated Indians not capable of fee patents. Most Indians incapable of farming more than 80 acres. Full-bloods would give better account of freedom than mixed-bloods if judiciously given. Mixed-blood failures showed full-bloods the quality of men assuming tribal leadership.

testimony.witness_title: Field Matron, St. Xavier, Crow Reservation
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.subject: Individual case reports of fee patent Indians
testimony.key_claims: Provided detailed individual cases: Joseph Cooper sold land, lives in tent. Henry Reid sold land, bought automobile. Thomas LaForge has patent but not sold land. Ralph Saco sold land, lost car and land. Ben Gardner sold land near oil well cheaply. Mary Takes The Gun has not sold. Amy Scott lost cattle ranch through mortgages. Olive R. Venne mortgaged home, items sold at sheriff's sale. Mary Humphrey benefited from citizenship. Two Indians who died had mortgaged places. Richard Wallace did not want a patent.

testimony.witness_title: Baptist Missionary, Lodge Grass, Crow Reservation
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.subject: Opinion on releasing Indians from government supervision
testimony.key_claims: Not in favor of turning all Indians loose at once but major portion would benefit from being cut off from government control. Indians will never learn to paddle own canoe on government transport. Most Crows with patents don't make good use of land or money but follow natural human course. Old Indians should remain wards. Some Crows refused citizenship to escape paying taxes. Some Indians should be forced to accept citizenship. Citizenship should be conferred as soon as possible on all except old Indians.

testimony.witness_title: Field Clerk, United States Indian Service, Tulsa, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.subject: Status of fee patent Indians in Cherokee and Creek territory
testimony.key_claims: Can think of only a few fee patent Indians in district holding lands and farming. Some who recently received patents have taken no action. In Tulsa, Creek and Washington counties, practically all half-bloods turned loose. About 100 Indians of more than half-blood turned loose through competency commissions. About 25 through departmental removal. Large percentage of latter made good use of property, more successful than average white man. Half-bloods had all restrictions on surplus allotments removed by Act of Congress, very small percent retained lands.

testimony.witness_title: Field Clerk, United States Indian Service, Durant, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.subject: Five Civilized Tribes property handling and competency policy
testimony.key_claims: Department's intention is betterment of race but red tape and theoretical methods cause more dependency. No distinction made between various tribes. Five Civilized Tribes never rebelled, follow every vocation. Not in favor of blanket removals. Worker Indians more successful than educated ones without work ethic. About 60% released from competency commission sold or mortgaged property. About 80% doing better than before release. Question whether Indian better off with restricted land he won't work or having sold it and compelled to work. Recommended unconditional removal for able-bodied Indians age 21-35 with eighth grade education. Cited inefficiency of three-tier bureaucratic process for restriction removal. Recommended protecting homestead 40 acres. Restrictions to be automatically removed in 1931.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, United States Indian Service, Shawnee, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.subject: Case of Mack Johnson, Kickapoo Indian
testimony.key_claims: Mack Johnson given patent to 40 acres worth $3000-$4000, his only remaining property except quarter interest in 80 acres. Land sold, money spent, mortgage pending on team, tools, stock. Sold mortgaged property, took money to Mexico, died there leaving wife and small children destitute. Missionary and white neighbors furnishing food. Agent who recommended patent bore larger blame for putting him out of business. Indians see agent as responsible for their ruin.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, formerly Standing Rock, North Dakota
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee policy
testimony.subject: History and results of patent-in-fee issuance at Standing Rock
testimony.key_claims: About 600 patents-in-fee issued at Standing Rock beginning with mixed-bloods prior to 1915. Very few early recipients retained land; became involved in mortgages that consumed resources. Only one Indian personally known who regained allotment after mortgaging. 1916 issuance to mixed-bloods who were as educated and competent as white people - practically all land disposed of. Many women married to white men immediately disposed of lands. Competency Commission dealt with those successful in industrial work and returned soldiers - fair percentage retained lands. Children allotted 50-70 miles from parents had no use for distant land and sold for practical reasons, often wisely spending money on cattle and improvements.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Fort Peck Indian Reservation (formerly Standing Rock)
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on fee patent policy
testimony.subject: Effects of patent-in-fee policy on Standing Rock Indians
testimony.key_claims: Earlier patentees (1916, mixed-blood) lost nearly all land through mortgages; only one Indian regained allotment. Subsequent Competency Commission patents dealt with those successful in industrial work and returned soldiers; fair percentage retained lands. Children allotted 50-70 miles from parents' homes had no use for land and sold it; money often wisely spent on cattle and improvements. Inheritance resulted in Indians owning more scattered land than they could use. Land speculators and unscrupulous white men tempted Indians. Believes policy was overall beneficial; degree of blood not a measure of competency; most successful citizen Indians are more than one-half Indian blood. Recommends individual merit assessment, not class distinction. Opposes leasing of home allotments.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on fee patent policy
testimony.subject: Conditions of fee patent Indians at Cheyenne River
testimony.key_claims: Has kept close tab on patent-in-fee Indians; a check-up will be convincing that too liberal a policy has been adopted. General condition of fee patent Indians considerably worse than before sale of their land. Indians not satisfied with freedom because expecting more money. Personally not satisfied with results.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Cheyenne River Agency, Whitehorse District
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry
testimony.subject: Status of 57 citizen Indians in Whitehouse District
testimony.key_claims: Of 57 citizen Indians, 45 have sold lands and 12 are holding theirs. High percentage of those who disposed of lands have little to show for sale money. A few used money for home improvements. Others holding patents. Better for Indians to work their land than lease it. Young Indians should be made citizens while young to learn responsibility.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Cheyenne River Agency, Promise, South Dakota
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry
testimony.subject: Release of Indians from Federal control
testimony.key_claims: Government released Indians and breeds from Federal control too suddenly; was a shock to them. Majority of first fee patent Indians sold all lands and spent money. After becoming citizens they conducted themselves as bad white men. County authorities began making assessments valuing grazing lands as farm lands, resulting in high taxes. Recommends individual examination with each Indian receiving patent with 20 acres held in trust as homestead. Allotments were originally 640 acres for heads of families as grazing land with 25-year trust period.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry
testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee policy at Pine Ridge
testimony.key_claims: Indiscriminate granting of patents would be disastrous to Indians and State. 341 patents issued April 1918 to those with less than half Indian blood; 370 patents September 1919 to half or less blood. Approximately 10% free from debt, 15% more with mortgages ranging half to two-thirds of land value. Tendency of Indians to convert lands to cash immediately. Indians who disposed of lands now living on relatives' or friends' lands. Turning all Indians loose would result in quick dissipation and pauperism. Recommends holding portion of allotment in trust indefinitely and patenting remainder. Land is fundamental wealth that must be conserved. Much dissatisfaction due to supervision over moneys and property.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Pine Ridge Reservation, Eagle Nest District
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry
testimony.subject: Conditions of fee patent Indians by blood degree
testimony.key_claims: Half-blood Indians with patents mostly in fair circumstances and doing nicely. Less than half-blood in class with white people, mostly have good homes, many married to whites. Full-bloods and more than half-blood are mixed lot, easily influenced, often revert to old customs, sell land, become lawless. Middle-aged are more industrious. Does not believe in turning all adult Indians loose at this time. Recommends holding at least 160 acres in trust and selling surplus under supervision.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Pine Ridge Indian Reservation, Anderson, South Dakota
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry
testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee policy results
testimony.key_claims: Very few cases where fee patent Indians are better off financially. About one-fourth have sold no land and are accumulating property. About one-fourth sold part and used money for livestock and machinery; some purchased other lands. About one-half sold lands with little to show. Recommends withholding patents due to poor financial conditions and low land prices not equal to appraised valuation.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Pine Ridge Reservation, Oglala, South Dakota
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry
testimony.subject: Individual case examples and policy recommendations
testimony.key_claims: Indians try to sell land for cash and stock upon receiving patent; if cannot sell, they mortgage and money is wasted. Cited Leroy Cuny (age 39, citizen, disposed of land, nothing to show, children cared for by others) and William Twiss (age 58, cannot read, retained land, 300 cattle, farms large scale, successful). Recommends individual case assessment; some Indians who appear incompetent are most competent. Government has been a little lax. Recommends retaining 160 acres under trust; 10-20 acres insufficient in this country.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Pine Ridge Indian Reservation, Wakpamni District
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry
testimony.subject: Conditions of fee patent Indians in Wakpamni District
testimony.key_claims: With exception of three Indians, all fee patent Indians in district are in much worse condition than before release from Federal control. Three exceptions retained land, have small herds, farm small scale, contented. Others sold all allotments, spent money on automobiles and riotous living, generally dissatisfied, seeking more government money. Recommends releasing young able-bodied educated Indians and holding quarter section for home site with sale proceeds held in trust.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Pine Ridge Indian Reservation, Porcupine, South Dakota
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry
testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee Indians conditions
testimony.key_claims: Does not know of any patent-in-fee Indians who have done exceedingly well. Others' receiving patents has been great detriment. Those turned loose seem satisfied with what has been done. Some are competent but avoid patents to avoid taxes. Recommends individual examination with superintendent and farmers passing on Indians regarding release from supervision. Would hold back not less than 160 acres as reservation not adapted for farming.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Pine Ridge Indian Reservation, Kyle, South Dakota
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry
testimony.subject: Policy on releasing Indians from supervision
testimony.key_claims: Quite a number have done exceedingly well, others have done nothing. Few have retained all land and are making good but represents small number who were doing well before patents issued. Some sold part and improved homes, others sold with nothing to show. Some want to be wards again, especially older ones; young ones are worse as they sell land and will not work. Would look into each case separately. Some need protection, some are competent but avoid patents for tax reasons.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry
testimony.subject: Report on 303 fee patents at Shoshone Reservation
testimony.key_claims: 303 patents-in-fee issued 1907-1930; average allotment 80 acres of good irrigable agricultural land. About 90% have either sold or mortgaged their lands. Few made beneficial use of proceeds for livestock and equipment. Majority squandered lands in extravagant living and automobiles. Many went broke and settled to work for wages. Fee patent Indians in worse shape financially than before. Education not sole basis for competency; ignorant full-blood may be as competent as educated breed. Reservation environments are great drawback. Favors entire removal of restrictions for competent Indians. Reservation of 10-40 acres for home would leave Indian part bond/part free. Recommends industrial education and withdrawal of charitable aid.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners survey on patents-in-fee
testimony.subject: Results of 303 patents-in-fee at Shoshone Reservation
testimony.key_claims: 303 patents issued 1907-1930 covering average 80-acre allotments of good irrigable agricultural land. Blood quantum breakdown: 1 full-blood, 3 three-fourths, 2 five-eighths, 5 one-half, 2 three-eighths, 3 one-fourth, 7 five-sixteenths, 9 one-eighth, and others. About 90% sold or mortgaged lands. Few made beneficial use of proceeds for livestock and agricultural equipment; majority squandered in extravagant living and automobiles. Recommended holding back at least 160 acres. Reservation not adapted for farming. Recommended great caution in granting patents to females as husbands squander property, desertions frequent, women left with children. Those who went broke and settled down to work for wages made better showing than on allotments. Reservation environments are the great drawback.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners survey on patents-in-fee
testimony.subject: Effects of patents-in-fee at Cheyenne & Arapaho Agency
testimony.key_claims: In practically every case lands have been sold. Many used money unwisely but possibly a majority used proceeds for some benefit - improvement of other lands or investment in business. On the whole believes it has been beneficial to give able-bodied competent Indians their patents. Agency officials do not follow up Indian activities after patent issued. Indians resent follow-up efforts. Recommended examining each individual case as to age, opportunity and physical capacity. If mentally and physically competent, favored turning them loose. Indians are no different than any other race regarding extravagance.

testimony.witness_title: United States Indian Farmer, Yankton Indian Reservation
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners survey on patents-in-fee
testimony.subject: Views on releasing Santee and Yankton Sioux from supervision
testimony.key_claims: As long as Indian's land held in trust he will never take his place in affairs of life among white brothers. Every young able-bodied Indian whose mind is functioning properly should have everything turned over unrestricted. Opposes reserving part of allotment as compromise. Indian should be either full citizen or ward. Does not know a single Santee Indian who received patent to entire allotment and still owns all of it. Among Yankton Sioux a few cases of patentees who still own all land and built good homes. Most disposed of land and used money in riotous living. Sooner they are broke and have to work the better. Identified Joseph Ellis and Thomas Hunter of Lake Andes as doing well; Simon Vasser and Gilbert St. Pierre among those who sold.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners survey on patents-in-fee
testimony.subject: Detailed report on patents-in-fee at Yankton Sioux reservation
testimony.key_claims: 599 patents to entire allotments and 13 for portions issued. Not more than 10 own entire original allotments; not more than 50 own any portion. Practically 550 disposed of all land; about 400 have absolutely nothing to show. Originally 3113 allotments comprising 368,400 acres; today not exceeding 59,000 acres held in trust. Allotments varied 80-320 acres. Mixed-bloods obtained twice the land through sharp practice of having agricultural land classified as grazing. Indians typically sell immediately after patent; within 12 months have nothing. Principal squandering through automobile purchases and joy-riding. White men beset Indians upon patent receipt to buy land at inadequate prices. About 60% of able-bodied members farming to some extent. Believes in issuing patents to entire allotments rather than partial. One of great mistakes is leaving impression that US is still responsible after release. Transitory period of suffering is necessary.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners survey on patents-in-fee
testimony.subject: Patents-in-fee effects and competency policy at Rosebud Agency
testimony.key_claims: More than 17,000 Indians received patents since 1917 nationally. Opposes granting patents 'in the bulk.' Each case should be decided on own merits irrespective of blood status or educational qualifications. Approximately 600 of allotments under agency received patents. About 90% immediately sold or mortgaged lands. 85% of tracts were 160 acres, valued $1000-$16000, average $4000 per quarter. Not one in ten Indians purchases teams, farm implements, or makes improvements. An Indian capable of earning living may still be classified as competent even if he wastes property proceeds. Recommends Office outline standard for competency commissioners and superintendents.

testimony.subject: Policy on issuing patents-in-fee to Indians
testimony.key_claims: Nine out of ten Indians who received patents sold their land and spent proceeds within one or two years. Nearly all bought cars after selling land. Not more than one in ten purchased teams, farm implements, or made improvements. About 600 out of 5,500 population received patents, principally in past ten years. 85% of patents covered 160 acres valued $1,000-$16,000, average $4,000. About 12-15 Indians still retain allotments. Recommended case-by-case evaluation irrespective of blood status or education. Warned against rushing process and cautioned about creating homeless paupers.

testimony.subject: Effect of patent-in-fee policy on Turtle Mountain Indians
testimony.key_claims: Government has gone too swiftly in issuance of patents-in-fee. 95% of Indians sold land as soon as they could, often at prices below real value or mortgaged it. Indians who mortgage land become discouraged, default on payments, and lose the land. Civilization should be reckoned in terms of generations. Recommended careful investigation of character and habits, with 20-40 acres held in trust for lifetime. Provided tabulation showing 1,393 patents covering 185,918.76 acres issued 1910-1921. About 3,500 Indians on reservation out of 3,400 enrolled. Allotments located in western North Dakota and eastern Montana because reservation only two townships.

testimony.subject: Condition of patent-in-fee Indians
testimony.key_claims: Indians are being released from federal supervision too rapidly. Their inability to handle business in competition with experienced white men places them at great disadvantage. Nearly all patent-in-fee Indians known to him are in worse condition than when they became independent citizens. Taxes on Indian reservations are necessarily high, exceed land income, making Indians anxious to sell. Recommended modified merit system and holding at least half of valuable allotments in trust for lifetime as home site.

testimony.subject: Certificates of competency and fee patents at Bad River Reservation
testimony.key_claims: 399 original allotments patented through certificates of competency since 1913, plus 74 heirship certificates, totaling 373 certificates. Rate increased from 4 in 1913 to 88 in 1920. Approximately 1,600 allotted Indians on reservation. 98% of those granted certificates sold their land. 80-acre allotments on former virgin forest land sold for $300-$1,500, most under $500. Trust funds also turned over averaging around $1,000. Indian is cheerful loser with no regrets. Modern educated Indians should be turned loose. Aged and dependent class and minors should be protected. About $1 million remains in trust for aged and minor Indians. About 150 Indians employed at lumber company sawmill operating 27 years on reservation.

testimony.subject: Effect of fee patents on Nez Perce Indians
testimony.key_claims: About 500 fee patents issued to Nez Perces. Prima facie competent (young educated class) first to dispose of lands and squander proceeds. Older uneducated people holding onto lands, buying other lands, even purchasing at land sales in competition with white bidders. Several full-blood Nez Perces hold mortgages on white men's farms. One full-blood woman holds $13,000 mortgage on 480 acres and $1,000 mortgage on orchard tract. One young man spent $17,000. Of 300 fee patents issued last year, estimated 200 owners sold or mortgaged land. 1,400 Indians on reservation, not 50 earning all own living. Nez Perces never received government rations. Recommends superintendents submit lists rather than wholesale patent issuance. Paradox of incompetency of the competent and competency of the incompetent. Three-fourths of Indians are thrifty, sober, law-abiding. Trust period extended ten years for most older Indians. 30,000 acres under irrigation.

testimony.subject: Effect of granting patents-in-fee to Fort Peck Indians
testimony.key_claims: Vital mistakes made in handling Indian question. Opposed to granting citizenship to Indians in bulk. Each reservation and individual case should be decided on own merit. Every family should maintain a homestead. Fort Peck Indians allotted only twelve years ago and large number now own nothing. Only way they can acquire real estate is through inheritance. Referenced Rocky Boy Indians who roamed Montana for sixty years without reservation, became degraded, state petitioned for reservation for them - illustrating that freedom alone does not lead to self-sufficiency. Referenced Fort Belknap reservation where Indians hold land in common and live in severe poverty despite splendid reservation.

testimony.witness_title: Field Clerk, Idabel, Oklahoma; member of Choctaw tribe
testimony.hearing: Investigation Committee for the House Committee of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Extension of restriction period for Choctaw Indians and protection of Indian property
testimony.key_claims: Testified that extension of restriction period would be entertained only in case of absolute necessity; emphasized that failure to provide protection would further interests of those seeking to separate Indians from their property; expressed great concern about approaching 1931 termination of Choctaw restrictions

testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee policy and Indian competency
testimony.key_claims: Three-fourths of Nez Perce Indians are thrifty, sober and law abiding; Rocky Boy Indians demonstrate that 60 years of freedom without supervision led to degradation and poverty; opposed granting citizenship to Indians in bulk; recommended each case be considered on its own merit; in four years allowed patents-in-fee to practically all young and middle aged people asking but only recommended portions of allotments; in great majority of cases patentees did nothing; Indians have lived on children's moneys for four years and refuse to work; of 196 patents issued, 36 have nothing left, 13 built homes, 56 retained land

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Coeur d'Alene Indian Agency, Sorrento, Idaho
testimony.subject: Patents-in-fee policy and results at Coeur d'Alene Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Administration of Indian affairs is a trust or guardianship; government policy of rationing without requiring repayment pauperized American Indians; opposed patent-in-fee unless allottee has personally farmed and become self-supporting; of 139 patents-in-fee issued, 55 were to whites, 54 Indians sold or lost land through mortgages, 42 doing no good; one full-blood with little education purchased additional land and is farming successfully; usual practice when Indian receives patent is to mortgage the land; many Indians told him they wished they had never received their patent; automobile nearly as demoralizing to Indian as whiskey

testimony.subject: Results of releasing Creek and Seminole Indians from restrictions
testimony.key_claims: In Hughes County, 1600 mixed blood allotments valued at $1,040 each; very small percent received fair consideration; 75% of mixed-bloods defrauded of 70% of allotment value; total estimated loss $873,600 in Hughes County and $544,320 in Seminole County; described specific fraud cases including Mollie Johnson, Daniel Johnson, Adeline Grayson, and Henderson Arbor; land men commonly called grafters are demanding Indians be turned loose; honest hard-working farmers living among Indians do not want them turned loose; proper education is the only solution

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on Indian affairs
testimony.subject: Effects of removal of restrictions on Cherokee Indians
testimony.key_claims: Approximately 1600 restricted Indians including minors in his district. Restrictions removed through regular channels in about 60 cases, by competency commissions in 105 cases, and by Departmental order covering half-blood Indians in approximately 100 cases. 90% of those receiving removal through regular channels have prospered. About 60% of those freed by competency commissions have disposed of or encumbered their property. About 75% of half-blood Indians released by Departmental order have sold or mortgaged allotments. Education of the coming generation is the most important work. Removal of restrictions as a class proposition is not advisable. Cherokee restrictions expire in 1931 which is too soon and will pauperize hundreds of Indians.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on Indian affairs
testimony.subject: Effects of removal of restrictions on Creek, Cherokee and Choctaw Indians
testimony.key_claims: Has been in Indian Service about 10 years. About 200 Indians granted unconditional removal by competency commission and about 125 half-blood Indians by blanket order since 1918, representing about one-fifth of adult restricted Indians. Does not recall one case where removal materially benefited the Indian in terms of accumulating property. About 10% would be classed as a success. Favors individual case-by-case removal. The chief reason for failure is the inherent weakness of the full-blood Indian in moral fibre and susceptibility to influence. Recommends competency commission of at least two experienced men working with local field representatives.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on Indian affairs
testimony.subject: Results of competency commission work among Cherokee Indians
testimony.key_claims: Of 100 personally acquainted Indians who received removal of restrictions, 65 sold their land and dissipated proceeds. 35 either retain original allotment or lands purchased with sale proceeds. About 90% of successful cases are less than full-blood. Custom was to remove restrictions from only one family member at a time. If restrictions removed from all Indians in a county, within 1-2 years title to more than 90% of restricted Indian land would pass from them forever. Fewer removals should be made.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on Indian affairs
testimony.subject: Choctaw Indian conditions and removal of restrictions
testimony.key_claims: Indians own land in other counties where they have never lived and will never consent to live. That land should be sold or restrictions removed. Indians do not plan for the future but look backward. They are as content to live in a shack as a good home. Wholesale removal of restrictions should not be considered until Indians become imbued with desire to better living conditions. Restrictions should be removed from surplus land not being lived on. Each individual case should be decided on its merits regardless of blood or educational qualifications.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on Indian affairs
testimony.subject: Views on unconditional removal of restrictions from Creek, Cherokee and Choctaw Indians
testimony.key_claims: Has been in Indian Service since 1913 across multiple agencies. Unconditional removal would result in wreck and ruin of most restricted Indians. Restricted Indians live in Indian communities, withdrawn from white citizenship, do not speak or write English. Unconditional removal would invite hordes of land grafters. When an Indian can speak, read and write English he should be given full citizenship. Each individual case should be handled strictly on its merits.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on Indian affairs
testimony.subject: Advisability of removing restrictions from Choctaw Indians
testimony.key_claims: Most Indians would soon get rid of their land and money if turned loose. Small percentage of full-bloods who attended government schools are making good. Best approach is to not turn loose too much at once. Recommends removing restrictions from 40-80 acres of surplus land at a time, selling it, and spending money through Indian Office. Some Indians who have been given control are doing well but they are part white. Some who profited from removal of restrictions are insisting full-bloods get restrictions removed so they can skin them.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on Indian affairs
testimony.subject: Advisability of removing restrictions from Choctaw Indians
testimony.key_claims: Five Civilized Tribes would be much better off if restrictions had never been removed. Knows several cases including himself where Indians have nothing to show for proceeds of allotment sales. Fully 80% have wasted all that was given to them. In another way, removal has made better citizens of some Indians as they are now contented to do honest labor. Worst enemy of Indians is whiskey and various liquors. Removal of all restrictions would mean a great deal of poverty.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on Indian affairs
testimony.subject: Conditions among restricted Chickasaw Indians
testimony.key_claims: Unconditional removal would be a sad mistake. There is always some grafter ready to buy, borrow, beg or steal anything the Indian has. Indians do not live to work, are easily influenced, and associates do not set good examples. Business men advise Indians to make bad investments when it benefits the white man. White men in the area want restrictions removed so Indians will pay taxes and work the roads. Cooperates with Department's present individual system of removal.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on Indian affairs
testimony.subject: Specific cases of land fraud against mixed-blood Indians and estimated total losses
testimony.key_claims: In Hughes County there were 1600 mixed blood allotments of 160 acres each, appraised at $1,040. Very small percent received fair consideration. Cited 9 specific cases of fraud. Estimated 75% of Hughes County mixed-bloods defrauded of 70% of allotment value ($873,600 total). In Seminole County, 90% of 630 mixed-blood Seminoles defrauded of 80% of allotment value ($544,320). Total district loss estimated at over $1.4 million. Jackson Wolf and wife declared competent despite inability to speak, read or write English. Colbert brothers disposed of allotments to buy garage with $20,000 mortgage. Only proper education of boys and girls can solve the problem. Competency commission is turning Indians loose inappropriately.

testimony.subject: Condition of restricted Choctaw Indians and advisability of removing restrictions
testimony.key_claims: Fully 80 percent of Indians who had restrictions removed have wasted all that was given to them and have nothing to show for any part of property sold. Worst enemy of Indians is whiskey and intoxicants. When drunk, Indians are 'relieved' of money by so-called friends. Some Indians who sold allotments have become contented to do honest labor. Five Civilized Tribes would be better off if restrictions had never been removed. Indians have full citizenship for voting and holding office. As Indians prove themselves competent they should be turned loose if they desire.

testimony.subject: Advisability of removing restrictions from Chickasaw Indians
testimony.key_claims: Indians do not live right to work, are easily influenced. Business men advise Indians to make bad investments when it benefits the white man. People who associate with Indians tell them Indian Service employees are just there for an easy job and are the ones doing the skinning. Removal of all restrictions would mean great poverty. Has not met a white man who would not like to see restrictions removed - they are jealous and want Indians to pay taxes and work roads.

testimony.witness_title: Agency Farmer, Colville Indian Reservation, Omak, Washington
testimony.subject: Success or failure of patent-in-fee policy on Colville Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Economic competency is not tangible possession like education or blood degree. Majority of Indians and whites lack excessive acquisitiveness. Believes in liberal policy for patents-in-fee. When Indian requests patent it argues financial incompetence or desire to obtain money through sale or mortgage. Out of approximately 90 fee patents, 40 would have made good under favorable conditions, 13 might have done reasonably well, rest would not have succeeded regardless. Extreme drought of past 4 years devastated both Indians and whites. Many Indians mortgaged land for farming equipment after patent but crop failures prevented success. Mrs. Mary Crook and Matilda Kruger refused patents. Recommends individual examination of each case.

testimony.witness_title: Agency Farmer, Colville Indian Reservation, Inchelium, Washington
testimony.subject: Benefits and disadvantages of patents-in-fee in Inchelium district
testimony.key_claims: District has larger percentage of mixed-blood Indians. Degree of blood has very little influence on whether patent was helpful or detrimental. Some full-bloods made good, some with little Indian blood dissipated allotments. Majority of cases were beneficial or not detrimental. Competent adults already received patents. Some who could get patents don't want them due to added taxation burden. Competency is more about natural ability than blood degree or literacy. Rising generation will change as they mingle with whites.

testimony.witness_title: Agency Farmer, Colville Indian Reservation, Nespelem, Washington
testimony.subject: Conditions of patent-in-fee Indians in Nespelem district
testimony.key_claims: Of 17 Indians in district, 11 sold allotments; only 3 have anything of value to show for money. In some cases disposition was justified because land was not agricultural and could not furnish a living. Detailed individual cases: Charley Bob energetic but in debt; Ross Hilleary sold land and bought car; Tom Andrews traded land for Ford car; Charley Hilburn traded for King Eight car; Sam Freidlander sold for $2500; William Friedlander making good with 100 acres; Bill Condon successful in stock raising; Whitelaw brothers successful; Pakatas boys' $10,000 each going fast.

testimony.witness_title: Agency Farmer, Fort Peck Agency, Poplar, Montana
testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee Indians on Fort Peck Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Patents issued without enough thought to future conditions. Most patent-in-fee Indians failed. Nearly all sold land, bought automobile, then farm machinery and stock. When cash gone, sold stock, machinery, then automobile. About 50% who received patents after board review are making good. Many dissatisfied - competent ones objected to citizenship because wanted tax exemption; others dissatisfied because lost heritage. Weather conditions past 4 years made success impossible. Indians living off children's money. Recommends homestead of 20-40 acres held in trust indefinitely. No patents issued without board review. Named successful cases: William Manning, David Manning, Francis and Alfred Murray, Daniel Courchene, Fred Bauer. Named failures: Joe Alvarez, John Anderson, John Bruguior, William Boyd.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Box Elder Sub-agency, Fort Peck Reservation, Brockton, Montana
testimony.subject: Conditions of patent-in-fee Indians on Fort Peck Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Patent-in-fee policy has been a failure to large extent on this reservation. Indians sell allotments outright, mortgage them for part cash and automobile, or trade them. Use automobile for joy-rides until all is spent. Present practice of issuing patents is too liberal. Conditions were far better before citizenship because of Government control preventing selling land. In those days Indians owned land and were self-supporting.

testimony.subject: Opinion on selling Indian land through Indian Office
testimony.key_claims: Would be governed by value of land. If poor rough land worth only a couple dollars an acre, no use to sell small tracts. In some cases might remove restrictions and let Indian sell with understanding that if money invested properly, more restrictions removed later. For old and feeble with no money, sell piece at a time and give money as needed. This practice should be done more.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Box Elder Sub-agency, Fort Peck Reservation
testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee conditions on Fort Peck Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Patent-in-fee issuance too liberal for Indians. Conditions far better before citizenship was given. Indians selling allotments outright or mortgaging for cash and automobiles. Recommended more careful examination and retaining homesteads.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Wolf Point Sub-agency, Fort Peck Indian Reservation
testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee conditions at Wolf Point
testimony.key_claims: Every Indian in district who received patent-in-fee has failed. No lands, no money, no homes. Some living with relatives for support, using children's money. Charles Owens sold 390 acres for $750 cash and livestock. Cleveland Owens sold 380 acres for horses and money. Ned and Lizzie Cantrell sold 740 acres and squandered money. Trust patent Indians like Henry Blacktail and Joshua Wets It have 40-80 head cattle and good homes. Recommended retaining at least 40 acres per individual.

testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee conditions in Blackpipe District
testimony.key_claims: 33 patents issued in 8.5 years. Some Larvie family members retained land. Full-bloods not successful with patents. Quarter breeds who retained land did better. 1913 patentees disposed of land immediately and spent money within 6 months. Recommended retaining 100 acres minimum and strenuous examination.

testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee conditions in Little White River District
testimony.key_claims: Almost all patent-in-fee Indians squandered land except four. First thing most do is get drunk and trade land for car and money. Those who sold bought automobiles used for joy-rides. Patent Indians come back to superintendent requesting patents on other allotments.

testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee conditions on Rosebud Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Great mistake to let Indians sell all land. Should be allowed to dispose of inherited lands but compelled to hold own allotment for another 35 years. Majority sell lands as fast as they get patent. Some mortgage land for old automobiles, lose land when unable to pay. Indian experience with money handling may do them good in time but they are very slow to learn.

testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee conditions, 800 patents issued, 10% success
testimony.key_claims: About 800 patents-in-fee issued on Rosebud. Not more than 10% made success. Large majority would have been far better off if land retained in trust. Of 21 patent-in-fee Indians in his district, only 3 did not sell. Fourteen of twenty-one sold lands and spent money. One sold for $6,200 and reinvested. One sold for $4,000 and partly reinvested. Recommended allowing sale of inherited lands through Office with supervision, retaining white settlement as good example.

testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee conditions, benefits of independence
testimony.key_claims: Indian will make no material progress until placed on own resources. Too much dependence on Government guardianship. After patent, Indians have nothing to sit and wait for. 90% squander land but then settle down. Knows dozens who squandered at least part but settled down and joined white community. Nearly all Indians more than half white made success. Cited full-blood typist employee who improved after receiving patent. 59 names submitted of benefited Indians. Recommended issuing fee patents for own land since children's lands still available.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer or official, Rosebud Indian Agency
testimony.subject: Individual examination and trust retention policy
testimony.key_claims: Strongly favors individual examination for each patent applicant. Many Indians realize they would be better off if property still held in trust. Recommends at least 40 acres retained in trust with clause compelling building of house and barn. Without restriction, Indians sell land or mortgage for one-third value, buy automobile, lose land when loan due. William Simpson and wife have no home, land sold. William Bordeaux and wife have no home, living hand to mouth. Todd Smith sold $13,000 of land, has only $300 house.

testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee conditions, learning through experience
testimony.key_claims: Believes more probability of Indians succeeding if they must depend on themselves. Cited full-blood young man who sold patent, bought car and stock, exhausted funds, returned to work and became best employee. Another full-blood sold two fee patents, using proceeds to improve wife's quarter. Indians sow wild oats then settle down.

testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee conditions, four years experience
testimony.key_claims: Grave question with as much against as for it. In four years knows few who did not sell and blow money. Small number making homes on land. Individual examination recommended. Should not turn all loose as most would be in poor house or begging, burden to state or county. Real estate men pester Indians until they sell.

testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee conditions on Standing Rock Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Approximately 600 patents-in-fee issued on Standing Rock. First issuance to mixed bloods and educated Indians before 1915 resulted in most immediately disposing of land. 1916 issuance largely to mixed blood element, practically all disposed of. Indians permitted themselves to be involved in mortgages. Only one Indian (Nation Flying) known to have made good. Many Indians received allotments 50-70 miles from parents' home, making land useless. Children allotted in 1908-1909 had no knowledge of their allotments. Many sold for no other reason than land was useless to them. White people felt administration period was one of private gain.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Effects of fee patents on Standing Rock Reservation Indians
testimony.key_claims: Approximately 600 patents in fee issued on Standing Rock. Pre-1915 patentees generally lost their land through mortgages with increasing principal and interest that ate up resources. 1916 patents went mostly to mixed bloods who were educated and competent but practically all disposed of their land. Only personally knows of one Indian from earlier patentees who regained his allotment. Children allotted 1908-1909 received land 50-70 miles from parents' homes they had never seen. Indians primarily interested in stock selected homes along waterways; subsequent allotments forced inland. Indians suddenly given resources fell prey to unscrupulous bankers and land speculators using unethical practices. Most successful citizen Indians are those of more than one-half Indian blood; those making most rapid land sales are mixed blood. Degree of blood is not a measure of competency. Allotments varied from 160 acres for unmarried Indians to 640 acres for heads of families. 90% of unmarried Indians received land miles from homes. Agricultural land valued at $20/acre (up to $30), while children's allotments worth only $10/acre. Recommended continuing fee patent issuance to competent Indians as only way for next generation to establish themselves among white men.
testimony.questioner: Board of Indian Commissioners via circular letter

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Patents-in-fee on Yakima Reservation 1917-1920
testimony.key_claims: Provided table showing 1917-1920 patent cases: totals of 16, 19, 118, and 49 cases respectively with columns for mortgaged, sold, and retained. Large percentage of allotments were average agricultural or irrigable land. Some Indians disposed of land immediately; others first placed mortgages that were increased until full value received then deeds given. Spendthrift types bought automobiles and quickly depleted funds. Experience has sobered most Indians. Recommends fee patents for all adult able-bodied mixed-blood allottees and full-blood class of middle age who are sober and industrious. Also recommends patents for educated full-bloods aged 24-25 who read and write English, as family influence will otherwise retard development.
testimony.questioner: Board of Indian Commissioners via circular letter

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Effects of patents-in-fee on Yakima Indians after ten years of observation
testimony.key_claims: Indians with patents progressed more rapidly than under government jurisdiction because they recognize responsibility. They became more independent, less reliant on government. Children entered public schools with white children. Indian has been too much pampered and not sufficiently thrown on own resources. Government should continue protection for dependent people but treat them as wards. Present leasing system for restricted Indian lands is burdensome and not logical. Recommends fee patents for portion of original allotments, retaining reasonable acreage for home purposes.
testimony.questioner: Board of Indian Commissioners via circular letter

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Specific cases of patent-in-fee Indians on Yakima Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Named specific successful Indians (William Cree, James Olney, Oscar Olney, Hayes Burns) and those who sold land and spent money foolishly (Alex Arquette, Wesley, O.C. Olney, Simon Goudy, William Fiander, David Enias, Ira Taswicht, Lester Pearne, Hackett). Recommends examining each Indian for competency, holding back 20 acres as permanent homestead, and selling inherited land. For old incompetent Indians, hold original allotment during life and sell inherited land, keeping money in trust with monthly disbursement.
testimony.questioner: Board of Indian Commissioners via circular letter

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Indians who received patents-in-fee
testimony.key_claims: Does not think they are going too fast in releasing Indians from government protection. Indians' condition is improved since becoming citizens. Recommends holding or reserving 20 acres as home site. Does not think issuing patents to old people is advisable; hold original allotments in trust unless absolutely necessary for support.
testimony.questioner: Board of Indian Commissioners via circular letter

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Status of 1004 patent-in-fee Indians on Flathead Reservation
testimony.key_claims: 1004 Indians received patents-in-fee to original allotments plus 31 allotments patented to heirs, ranging from 80-160 acres. Patents issued from 1910-1921 totaling 1,025. Approximately 75% disposed of original allotments. Those retaining lands are progressive and successful farmers comparable to average white citizens. About 25% who lost land have settled down and make comfortable livings on leased lands or wages. Some most pronounced failures were young educated fellows and returned soldiers. Citizenship cannot safely be granted en masse; blood degree is no criterion. Attitude of local whites varies greatly - some localities helpful, others entirely predatory. Superintendent's judgment should be followed in recommending patents.
testimony.questioner: Board of Indian Commissioners via circular letter

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee Indians in Ronan area
testimony.key_claims: Indians doing same as before patents - successful ones still successful, those living off rents still trying to obtain rents. Where they sold allotments and dissipated proceeds they are working to secure passable living. Some always looking forward to tribal payments. Majority in Ronan securing living by farming, laboring, or business. Percentage of success about the same among Indians as whites. Recommends dealing with each case separately on merits.
testimony.questioner: Board of Indian Commissioners via circular letter

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Detailed case studies of patent-in-fee Indians in Polson area
testimony.key_claims: Many Indians sold allotments for less than appraised value and spent all money. Four families (Frank McLeod, Alex McLeod, Louis Clairmont Jr., Gilbert Burland) depending almost entirely on tribal payments. McLeods had good land under private water rights but moved to town, invested in automobiles, became penniless. Successful examples include Mary Duplessis (store), Duncan Campbell (feed barn/pool hall), Sam Pierre (farming/stock), Harry Burland (garage), Mose Delaware (farming/clerking), Edna Hull (nurse). Specific failures: Joseph R. sold allotment for $3000 spent in 3 weeks; Joseph Antiste broke in one month; Joseph Gardipie broke; Louison Ashley failed at saw mill and threshing. Some full-blood improvident Indians in good appearance would deceive anyone about their ability. Majority of Indians cannot be satisfied no matter what done for them.
testimony.questioner: Board of Indian Commissioners via circular letter

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.subject: Report from St. Ignatius District, Flathead Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Report on 78 of 133 patent-in-fee Indians in St. Ignatius District: 45 (58%) sold land and spent money, 22 (28%) retained land, 7 sold land and invested proceeds, 4 mortgaged their property.
testimony.questioner: Board of Indian Commissioners via circular letter

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on patent-in-fee Indians
testimony.subject: Status of patent-in-fee Indians in Polson district
testimony.key_claims: Listed specific cases: McLeods had good land but moved to town, bought cars, became penniless. Frank McLeod, Alex McLeod, Louis Clairmont Jr., Gilbert Burl depended on tribal payments. Several Indians sold allotments and became destitute (Joseph Antiste broke in one month, Joseph Gardipie broke, Louison Ashley failed at saw mill and threshing). Some exceptions: Fred Paricole got laundry work, Peter Gangras became reliable logger. Some Indians remained on allotments successfully: David Ashley, Victor Dupuis, Caville Dupuis farming well. Recommended patents for Indians one-half or less blood who had attained majority. Opposed reserving home sites as no Indian could make living on 10-20 acres.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry
testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee Indians experience
testimony.key_claims: In almost every case where a patent has been issued the Indian has gone backward for a length of time. Many realized necessity of being on guard after being losers of small amounts and are getting down to real business. Others chose automobiles and good times, completely out of money before realizing what happened. Indians are young husky fellows who will have some bad experiences in the beginning of citizenship. About 49 patent-in-fee Indians in district. About 20 have disposed of allotments. 33 doing fairly well. Recommended retaining small portion of allotment or inherited lands for good of Indian.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry
testimony.subject: Certificates of competency and patent-in-fee policy
testimony.key_claims: Approximately 80% of Indians who received certificates of competency sold their land; remaining 20% have mortgages, some going through foreclosure. Opposed issuing certificates of competency except in extreme cases. Found white people encouraging Indians to ask for certificates and advancing money on strength of having them turned over. Certificates provide easy method for Indians to sell heirship land. Better class of Indians do not want certificates. Recommended terminating all tribal fund claims when certificate issued. Would not issue certificate to Indians living on or near reservation.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Sisseton Agency, Sisseton, South Dakota
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry
testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee policy and Indian competency
testimony.key_claims: About half of reservation Indians are full-bloods. Negligible number who received patents retained their land. Main reason for seeking patent is to sell land. Proceeds spent on subsistence, clothing, automobiles. After selling land and losing government assistance, Indians typically leave reservation and find employment. Some Indians are parasites who will not work regardless of assistance. Policy should disregard blood or educational status and require Indians to demonstrate ability first. Cited Alex Renville as successful farmer. Named Joseph Flute, Taylor Flute, Smiley Williams, Stephen LaBelle, Elizabeth Hopkins, Smiley Finley, Edward Williams as those who squandered $10,000-$12,000 each in three years.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry
testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee policy at Potawatomi Agency
testimony.key_claims: 813 allotments made to Potawatomis on three rolls over 39 years. In 1918, 43 original allottees given patents by competency board. Approximately 100 obtained patents prior to 1914. Total about 177 patented. About one-third now deceased. 85% have sold land or mortgaged it to full value. 50% of money used paying old debts, remainder on automobiles, teams, wagons. Favors issuing patents to competent able-bodied Indians regardless of blood status. Opposed to competency boards. Indians who have to work are preferred by local farmers. Many admit government did its duty and they spent their own money.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Seger Indian Agency, Colony, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry
testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee results at Seger Agency
testimony.key_claims: Spring 1917 competency commission examined large number of Indians, result was exceedingly disastrous for every Indian who received patent. Most allotments disposed of, some at ridiculously low prices. Indians disposed of land immediately upon receipt of patent, contracts to sell likely existing prior to receipt. In charge since June 10, 1920. Recommended only one direct patent - allottee sold 80 acres for $6,000, bought home in Anadarko, deposited $1,500 with office. Absolutely opposed to issuing patents in wholesale manner. Better for restricted Indians to lease land rather than work it. Opposed to turning over property to Indians of one-half or less blood without careful consideration.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Cantonment Indian Agency, Canton, Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry
testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee policy
testimony.key_claims: Believed the practice of issuing fee patents was pernicious. Indians who received patents disposed of allotments immediately or very soon after receipt. Money spent for support. Those who disposed of allotments are practically without exception penniless and depend on relatives or inherited interests for livelihood.

testimony.subject: Status of fee patent Indians and land management
testimony.key_claims: About 25 fee patent Indians are holding their original allotments and farming them, except a few who hold good positions elsewhere. One-third of allottees are deceased and of the remaining two-thirds, all but ten or twelve still have land held under supervision. A competency commission in Spring 1917 examined a large number of Indians, with exceedingly disastrous results for every Indian who received a patent. Out of approximately 220+ allotments, land was disposed of at ridiculously low prices. Indians disposed of land immediately upon receipt of patent, with pre-existing contracts to sell. Believes restricted Indians are better off leasing land rather than working it themselves due to issues with loans and mortgages on crops. However, believes it is much better for Indians to farm their own land. States the trouble with the Indian race is too much money without effort. All able-bodied Indians are much better off when they have to work.

testimony.subject: Fee patents, Indian land management, and competency determinations
testimony.key_claims: Has been in charge since June 10, 1920, and recommended only one patent be issued direct during his tenure. That allottee sold 80 acres for $6,000 and purchased a home in Anadarko, also depositing $1,500 with the office. Believes issuing fee patents is a pernicious system. Indians who received patents disposed of their allotments immediately or very soon after receipt. Those who disposed of allotments are practically without exception penniless and depend solely on relatives or inherited interests for livelihood. Opposed to turning over property to Indians of one-half or less blood without careful consideration. Personally absolutely opposed to issuing patents in wholesale manner; believes each case should be considered on its merits regardless of quantum of Indian blood. Considers quantum of Indian blood no test of competency; the only fair test is education. States that older non-English speaking Indians should be protected during their lifetime, including from their own children and younger Indians. Advocates removing restrictions and forcing younger educated Indians to work, believing they will otherwise become helpless and beyond redemption. The average Indian will out-bargain and beat the average white man in business dealing.

testimony.subject: Conditions of Cheyenne and Arapaho Indians and fee patent outcomes
testimony.key_claims: Has lived and worked among Cheyenne and Arapaho Indians for seven years (three as agency farmer, four as lease clerk). Majority of Indians have disposed of or lost their allotments. Only a very few live on or cultivate a portion of their allotments, preferring to live in camps or villages. Lands cultivated are usually forage crops requiring little labor. Difficult to get Indians to work if they have money to their credit. Condition largely attributed to the custom of leasing lands rather than being taught or compelled to farm. Not a single Indian under this agency who obtained a patent has retained possession of lands any length of time; they held them no longer than required to effect a sale. Believes Indians returning from school have better education and training than average white children and are equally competent if properly trained. Argues that if Indians were given full responsibility upon reaching majority, most would succeed. Current system provides no incentives. Indians returning from school lose ambition within months and fall into ways of their fathers because government looks after their interests.
